The ones that learned are not the ones you are looking at.
To be fair, nobody ever showed them the green man.

premise: Support: 'Have you tried turning it off and on again?' Customer: 'Nine times so far.'

punchlines.text: Support: 'Then it is working as designed.'
Support: 'Try it a thousand more times and let me know.'
Support: 'Now turn yourself off and on again and see whether the screen notices.'
Support: 'The tenth one is the one that counts. Nobody knows why.'

premise: What do you call a customer service line that plays music at you for forty minutes?

punchlines.text: A single with no release date.
A waiting list with strings.
The hook.
By minute thirty-eight I knew the song, the arrangement, and the exact bar where the loop cuts off the ending.

premise: How many adults does it take to get a sofa up one flight of stairs?

punchlines.text: Three, and it still does not fit.
Four, plus the one who measured the stairwell and swore it would fit.

premise: Every recipe says the onions will be soft in five minutes, and they never are.

punchlines.text: Five minutes is not a length of time. It is a mood the writer was in.
I have stood over the same onions since Tuesday and they have started to form a plan.
The recipe is not lying. It is simply not a recipe for your stove.
Five minutes later the recipe says to add the garlic, which tells you exactly how much that writer knows about five minutes.

premise: Every project has one file that nobody will touch.

punchlines.text: It has no authors in the history, only survivors.
We call it legacy because somebody left it to us and then left.

premise: What's the difference between a marathon runner and a gym member?

punchlines.text: One measures progress in kilometres, the other in monthly direct debits.
One runs marathons. The other goes to a gym.
One of them has finished something this year, and it is not me.

premise: What's the difference between a concept album and a nervous breakdown?

punchlines.text: One of them comes with a gatefold sleeve.
Timing, and a producer.
One of them you can listen to again afterwards.
I made both in the same year and only one of them is on a shelf.

premise: Nobody tells you that a long marriage is mostly two people negotiating about a thermostat.

punchlines.text: The rest of it is deciding which one of you is going to call the plumber.
One of you will get up at three in the morning to move that thermostat back two degrees, every night, for forty years.

premise: People used to worry that machines would take all the boring jobs.

punchlines.text: Instead they took the painting, and left us the forms.
Now the machines do the worrying, and we watch them do it.
It turns out the machines found our jobs boring too.

premise: A man takes a broken toaster back to the shop with the receipt, the box, and all of the packaging.

punchlines.text: The assistant asked whether he had tried turning it off and on again. It is a toaster.
They replaced it with a second toaster, which arrived broken, in the same box, with his own receipt inside.
They gave him store credit, which he will spend in that shop, on that toaster, in that way.
They said the packaging was not original. It was the box. It had the toaster's face printed on it.
They explained that the warranty covers manufacturing faults, not toast.

premise: A director shoots a three-hour film with no dialogue, no music and no cuts. The studio asks for exactly one change.

punchlines.text: They wanted it longer.
They asked him to add a scene where something happens.
They asked for a trailer, which is the version of this joke people would sit through.
They asked him to remove the camera.
They asked for a 4K remaster, so the audience could see nothing happening in greater detail.

premise: A dog walks into a vet's office, jumps onto the table by himself, and lies down.

punchlines.text: The vet says the dog has clearly done this before, and the owner agrees.
He hands over a form he filled in himself. Under 'symptoms' he has written 'the mailman'.
The vet examines him, finds nothing wrong, and the dog goes home.

premise: Nobody has ever met a person who enjoyed the chemistry lab safety briefing.

punchlines.text: The one person who did enjoy it is the reason we have one.
Forty minutes on goggles, and eleven seconds on the thing that can actually kill you.
Still, it was a reaction I will never forget.

premise: My manager told me to think outside the box.

punchlines.text: I thought outside the box, and now I am thinking outside the payroll.
So I stood outside with the recycling and waited for a better idea.
I said the phrase itself is the box, and now I am on a performance plan.
I thought so far outside the box that I ended up at a different company, which is where I am now.

premise: I joined a book club that reads the last page first.

punchlines.text: We finished the year in four minutes and spent the rest of it arguing about how we got there.
It is the only club where I have not fallen behind.
It ruins the books. Endings are the part that has to be last.

premise: I bought a weather app that promises to be honest with me.

punchlines.text: This morning it said 'grey', and then it added 'and so are you'.
It has said 'probably' every day for six weeks.
It now only shows the number of warm days I have left.
It has started giving me the forecast for the places I said I would visit and never did.
There is a real climate of trust about it.

premise: Every office has one person who reads the whole survey before answering it.

punchlines.text: They are the only one who actually answers it properly.
They found three leading questions, one broken scale, and the name of the consultant.
I am not that person. I am the person who picks the middle box for everything.
The rest of us are what the report politely calls the response rate.

premise:
Friend: "You really should start investing."
Me: "With what?"

punchlines.text: "With the rent money. Rent is optional if you are brave."
"Ten dollars a month. In forty years, at seven percent, that is very nearly a good dinner."
"Time. You have less of it than you think, and it compounds the other way."

premise:
"What is your novel about?"
"It is very hard to summarize."

punchlines.text: Try. You have had nine years.
That is all right. I was not really going to read it anyway.

premise: 'The doctor says I have to cut down on salt, sugar, and stress.' 'What did you say?'

punchlines.text: 'I said I could manage two of the three, and asked which two he would pick.'
'Nothing. I was eating.'
'I asked what happens if I keep all three, and he wrote something down instead of answering.'
'I said that sounds like the setup to a joke, and he said the punchline is usually the bill.'

premise: Everyone wants to go to Mars until you describe a Tuesday there.

punchlines.text: It is the same as Monday, plus forty minutes.
The good news is that the commute is short and permanent.
It is red, it is far away, and it is not very nice.
Nine months in a metal tube with four colleagues, and one of them brings a guitar.

premise: Nobody in this city agrees on anything except which street to avoid.

punchlines.text: Every one of them is on that street right now, agreeing.
There are four such streets, and a local will name all of them, unprompted, for nine minutes.

premise: Every song you loved at seventeen sounds like a letter from somebody who owes you money.

punchlines.text: You can hear yourself in there, promising things.
And he is dead now, so that money is gone for good.
Mine mostly owes me an apology for the haircut.
